learning_objective: 🎯 Learn how sheer determination, willpower, and step-by-step practice can help anyone conquer their deepest, most paralyzing fears!

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Douglas developed a fear of water at age 3 or 4 when he was knocked down by a powerful wave at a beach in California, leaving him breathless and terrified.
At age 10 or 11, Douglas tried to learn swimming at the YMCA pool. A strong, older boy threw him into the deep end (9 feet) as a joke, nearly causing Douglas to drown.
While sinking, Douglas planned to hit the bottom and jump back up like a cork. However, the water paralyzed him. He experienced stark terror, went down three times, and finally passed out.
Years later, tired of being deprived of fishing and canoeing, he hired an instructor. The instructor used a belt and pulley system to safely rebuild Douglas's confidence, teaching him piece by piece.
To ensure the fear was completely dead, Douglas swam in Lake Wentworth and Warm Lake alone. He realized that 'all we have to fear is fear itself' (quoting FDR).

fun_activity.title: 🧱 Build It Piece by Piece
fun_activity.instructions: The instructor made Douglas a swimmer 'piece by piece' (breathing first, kicking next). If you had to learn how to juggle 3 balls, what would be your 'piece by piece' step 1, step 2, and step 3?

exam_tips: 📌 Describe the physiological and psychological symptoms of Douglas's terror when drowning: lungs aching, head throbbing, paralyzing fear, and eventual peaceful oblivion.
📌 Distinguish between the two separate incidents that caused his fear: The California beach (age 3/4) and the YMCA pool (age 10/11).
📌 Highlight Roosevelt’s quote: 'All we have to fear is fear itself.' It means the actual dying is peaceful; it is the *fear* of death that causes terror.
quick_recap: ⭐ The Yakima River was treacherous and had caused many drownings, which is why his mother warned him against it.
⭐ The instructor took 6 months to train him, but Douglas took even longer to independently test himself in open lakes.
⭐ Overcoming his fear gave Douglas a profound appreciation for life and an intense desire to live fully.
